section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Directed Area
section_1.content: Briefly revisit the 2D determinant representing the signed area of a parallelogram. Introduce the leap to 3D by defining the cross product as a vector perpendicular to the plane formed by two input vectors, with a magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram they span.
section_1.example: Imagine a robotic arm moving two rods; the 'sweep' between them creates a flat shape whose orientation and size define our new vector.

section_2.title: Geometric Intuition: The Right-Hand Rule
section_2.content: Visualize the cross product as a physical orientation. Use the Right-Hand Rule to explain how the order of vectors (a × b vs b × a) flips the direction of the resulting vector, emphasizing its role as a 'normal' vector.
section_2.example: Use a character, 'Agent Vector', pointing fingers to show how the thumb always points 'up' relative to the floor spanned by the index and middle fingers.

section_3.title: Linear Transformations & Change of Volume
section_3.content: Connect the cross product to the concept of the Scalar Triple Product. Explain how the cross product is not just a vector, but a tool to compute the signed volume of a parallelepiped, which represents the determinant of a 3D linear transformation.
section_3.example: An animation of a 3D cube morphing into a slanted prism: the volume change is quantified by the interaction of the cross product of the base vectors with the third vector.

section_4.title: Application: The Physical World (Torque)
section_4.content: Apply the cross product to physics. Define Torque (τ = r × F). Show how the cross product captures the 'leverage' effect—where only the component of force perpendicular to the radius arm causes rotation.
section_4.example: A squirrel trying to open a round nutcracker: the force applied at the tip (r) creates rotation based on the cross product with the force vector (F).

section_5.title: Summary & Synthesis
section_5.content: Recap: Cross product = Direction (Normal) + Magnitude (Area). It serves as the fundamental bridge between geometric configuration and the volume-scaling nature of linear operators.
section_5.example: A quick visual recap showing the transition from two lines on a screen to a 3D volume, linking the 'Area' concept back to the 'Linear Transformation' concept.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Map to right side of screen
